hops.afterHeading: Three ways to organize a signal
hops.title: The transplant drug that came out of Easter Island dirt
hops.text: During a 1964-65 Canadian expedition to Easter Island, microbiologist Georges Nogrady collected more than 200 soil samples from across the island. One of them yielded a bacterium that makes a compound named for the island's own name, Rapa Nui: rapamycin. When Ayerst closed its Montreal lab, Suren Sehgal kept the strain in his home freezer, against company directives, and the work restarted in 1988 after Ayerst merged with Wyeth; the FDA approved the drug in 1999. Rapamycin catalyzes nothing. It grips the small protein FKBP12, and that pair clamps the growth kinase mTOR. An adaptor the size of a drug.

hops.title: More of a bridge can mean less bridging
hops.text: A PROTAC is a lab-built molecule with two ends: one grips a disease-linked protein, the other grips an enzyme that tags proteins for the cell's disposal machinery. It is easy to assume that more of the bridge means more clearing. In cell experiments, some PROTACs clear the most target at middling concentrations; raise the concentration further and separate PROTAC molecules can cap each partner on its own, so fewer complete sandwiches form and clearing can drop. Chemists call the dip the hook effect; immunologists met the same bell-shaped curve in 1905 antibody tests and called it the prozone.

sources.citation: Ghosh SB et al. Exosome-mediated delivery of PROTACs for targeted protein degradation in cancer, neurodegenerative, infectious, and inflammatory diseases. J Cell Mol Med. 2026;30(15):e71297.
Douglass EF Jr, Miller CJ, Sparer G, Shapiro H, Spiegel DA. A comprehensive mathematical model for three-body binding equilibria. J Am Chem Soc. 2013;135(16):6092-6099.

image.caption: At high doses, separate two-ended molecules can grab each partner alone, so a middling dose can work best.

hops.title: Yeast that answered a mating signal with a salt response
hops.text: Budding yeast keep romance and salt emergencies apart, even though the mating pathway and one branch of the salt-stress pathway share the kinase Ste11. In 2003 Sang-Hyun Park, Ali Zarrinpar and Wendell Lim fused Ste5, the mating scaffold, to Pbs2, the salt-stress one, and mutated away the hybrid's links to the usual salt input and the usual mating output. In yeast lacking the native scaffolds and a second salt-sensing branch, cells with the hybrid survived high salt only when given mating pheromone, and could no longer mate. Pheromone in, salt response out. The hybrid still needed Pbs2's own kinase activity, so what changed was which partners the organizer connects.

sources.citation: Park SH, Zarrinpar A, Lim WA. Rewiring MAP kinase pathways using alternative scaffold assembly mechanisms. Science. 2003;299(5609):1061-1064.
Good MC, Zalatan JG, Lim WA. Scaffold proteins: hubs for controlling the flow of cellular information. Science. 2011;332(6030):680-686.

audio.title: A freezer in Montreal, a fly on the table, and some confused yeast
audio.transcript: It is easy to assume that the real work of cell signaling belongs to the enzymes, like the kinases that move phosphates around. The binding proteins that only hold partners together can sound like quiet stagehands. Here are three true stories where the stagehands run the show. Start with a home freezer in Montreal. Inside were samples of a soil bacterium that came from a Canadian expedition to Easter Island, which began in December nineteen sixty-four. On that trip, the Montreal microbiologist Georges Nogrady collected more than two hundred soil samples from across the island. One of those isolates reached Suren Sehgal and his colleagues at Ayerst Laboratories, who found that the bacterium made a remarkable compound. They called it rapamycin, after Rapa Nui, the island's own name. When the company closed its Montreal research facility, Sehgal took samples of the bacterium home and kept them in his freezer, against company directives. After Ayerst merged with Wyeth, he got the rapamycin research going again in nineteen eighty-eight. In nineteen ninety-nine, the F D A approved rapamycin to help prevent rejection after kidney transplants. Here is the part that matters for this lesson. Rapamycin has no enzyme activity at all. It works as a tiny chemical adaptor, what chemists now call a molecular glue. It grips a small cell protein called F K B P twelve, and that pair together clamps onto a growth kinase called M tor. The drug's whole trick is forcing two proteins to meet, and the new partnership makes it harder for M tor to reach some of the proteins it normally acts on. Now move from a freezer to your kitchen table, where a housefly is sitting beside your sandwich. Wave a hand at it slowly and watch how easily it leaves. Fly vision runs what researchers have called the fastest G-protein signaling cascade known. In experiments, the quickest housefly responses to a flash or a looming shape took about thirteen to twenty milliseconds. Flies also notice flicker we cannot. In lab tests, male green bottle flies landed most often on lights flashing about one hundred seventy-eight times a second, the wing-flash rate of young females in flight. In fruit flies, researchers found a scaffold called Ina D that helps organize the eye's fast response to light. It uses five P D Z domains to hold the light-activated ion channel and its partner enzymes right next to each other, instead of letting them find each other by drifting. When researchers disrupted one particular grip, the complex came out missing its ion channel; disrupt another, and it lost an enzyme instead. Finally, can you rewire a living cell by rebuilding a scaffold? In two thousand three, Sang-Hyun Park, Ali Zarrinpar and Wendell Lim tried it in budding yeast. The mating pathway and one branch of the high-salt pathway share a kinase called Ste eleven. The researchers fused the mating scaffold, Ste five, to the salt-stress scaffold, P B S two, and mutated away the links to the usual salt input and the usual mating output. In yeast lacking their own two scaffolds and a second salt-sensing branch, cells with the hybrid survived high salt only when they got mating pheromone, and they could no longer mate. Pheromone in, salt response out. The hybrid needed both the new connections and the kinase activity of P B S two. Binding proteins do not run all the chemistry. By deciding who meets whom, and where, they write the wiring diagram.
